Que.q: Q1 : What is Spring Boot?
Que.a: Spring Boot is an open-source framework built on top of the Spring Framework that simplifies the development of Java applications. It reduces configuration complexity by providing auto-configuration, embedded servers, and starter dependencies. Developers can quickly create production-ready applications with minimal setup and boilerplate code. Spring Boot is widely used for building REST APIs, microservices, and enterprise applications because it improves development speed, simplifies deployment, and integrates seamlessly with the Spring ecosystem while following convention-over-configuration principles.

Que.q: Q2 : What are the Features of Spring Boot?
Que.a: Spring Boot provides several powerful features that simplify application development and deployment. It offers auto-configuration, starter dependencies, embedded servers, production-ready monitoring tools, and simplified configuration management. It supports rapid application development and integrates easily with databases, messaging systems, cloud platforms, and security frameworks. Spring Boot also provides actuator endpoints for monitoring application health and metrics. These features help developers focus on business logic rather than spending time configuring infrastructure and framework components manually.

Que.q: Q3 : What are the advantages of using Spring Boot?
Que.a: Spring Boot offers numerous advantages including reduced configuration effort, faster application development, and easier deployment. It eliminates the need for complex XML configurations and provides sensible defaults through auto-configuration. Embedded servers allow applications to run independently without external deployment. Spring Boot also supports microservices architecture, cloud-native development, monitoring, and testing. Its rich ecosystem and integration with other Spring projects make it an ideal choice for modern enterprise applications that require scalability, maintainability, and rapid development cycles.

Que.q: Q4 : Define the Key Components of Spring Boot.
Que.a: Spring Boot consists of several key components that work together to simplify application development. Starter dependencies provide predefined dependency bundles, auto-configuration configures beans automatically, and embedded servers enable standalone deployment. Spring Boot Actuator offers monitoring and management capabilities, while Spring Initializr helps generate project structures. Configuration files such as application.properties or application.yml manage application settings. Together, these components reduce boilerplate code and accelerate the development of robust and production-ready Java applications.

Que.q: Q5 : Why do we prefer Spring Boot over Spring?
Que.a: Spring Boot is preferred over traditional Spring because it significantly reduces configuration effort and accelerates development. Traditional Spring applications require extensive XML or Java-based configuration, whereas Spring Boot provides auto-configuration and starter dependencies. It includes embedded servers that eliminate the need for external deployment containers. Spring Boot also offers built-in monitoring, easier testing, and simplified dependency management. These features allow developers to focus on implementing business logic instead of spending time on infrastructure and framework setup.

Que.q: Q6 : Explain the internal working of Spring Boot.
Que.a: Spring Boot starts by executing the main method that invokes SpringApplication.run(). It creates and initializes the Spring Application Context, scans components, loads configuration files, and applies auto-configuration based on available dependencies. Starter dependencies provide required libraries, while embedded servers such as Tomcat are automatically configured. Spring Boot also registers beans, applies dependency injection, and starts web services if required. This automated startup process allows applications to be configured and executed with minimal manual intervention from developers.

Que.q: Q7 : What are the Spring Boot Starter Dependencies?
Que.a: Spring Boot Starter Dependencies are predefined dependency packages that bundle commonly used libraries together. Instead of manually adding multiple dependencies, developers can include a single starter dependency to obtain all required components. Examples include spring-boot-starter-web for web applications, spring-boot-starter-data-jpa for database access, and spring-boot-starter-security for security features. Starter dependencies simplify dependency management, ensure compatibility between libraries, and reduce configuration complexity, making application development faster and more reliable.

Que.q: Q8 : How does a Spring application get started?
Que.a: A Spring Boot application starts from the main class that contains the main() method. This method calls SpringApplication.run(), which bootstraps the application by creating the Spring Application Context. The framework scans packages for components, loads configurations, performs dependency injection, applies auto-configuration, and initializes required beans. If the application is a web application, an embedded servlet container such as Tomcat is started automatically. Once initialization completes, the application becomes ready to process incoming requests.

Que.q: Q9 : What does the @SpringBootApplication annotation do internally?
Que.a: The @SpringBootApplication annotation is a convenience annotation that combines three important annotations: @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan. It marks the class as a configuration source, enables automatic bean configuration based on dependencies, and scans packages for Spring-managed components. This single annotation significantly simplifies application setup by replacing multiple configuration annotations. It serves as the primary entry point for Spring Boot applications and enables most of Spring Boot's automatic features.

Que.q: Q10 : What is Spring Initializr?
Que.a: Spring Initializr is a web-based tool that helps developers quickly create Spring Boot projects with predefined configurations and dependencies. Users can select the project type, build tool, Java version, Spring Boot version, and required dependencies through a graphical interface. Spring Initializr then generates a ready-to-use project structure that can be imported into IDEs such as IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse, or VS Code. It significantly reduces project setup time and helps developers start building applications immediately.

Que.q: Q11 : What is a Spring Bean?
Que.a: A Spring Bean is an object that is created, managed, and maintained by the Spring IoC container. Instead of developers manually creating objects, Spring handles their lifecycle, dependency injection, configuration, and destruction. Beans are typically defined using annotations such as @Component, @Service, @Repository, and @Controller, or through Java/XML configuration. Spring Beans help achieve loose coupling, better maintainability, and easier testing by allowing dependencies to be injected automatically into application components.

Que.q: Q12 : What is Auto-wiring?
Que.a: Autowiring is a feature in Spring that automatically injects required dependencies into a bean without explicitly creating or passing objects. It reduces boilerplate code and simplifies dependency management. Spring resolves dependencies by type, name, or qualifier and injects the appropriate bean at runtime. The most common way to perform autowiring is through constructor injection, which improves immutability and testability. Autowiring helps build loosely coupled applications and allows developers to focus more on business logic rather than object creation.

Que.q: Q13 : What is ApplicationRunner in Spring Boot?
Que.a: ApplicationRunner is an interface provided by Spring Boot that allows developers to execute code immediately after the application context is loaded and the application has started successfully. It is commonly used for initialization tasks such as loading default data, validating configurations, or running startup logic. The run() method receives ApplicationArguments, making it easier to access command-line arguments in a structured way. ApplicationRunner executes before the application begins processing regular requests.

Que.q: Q14 : What is CommandLineRunner in Spring Boot?
Que.a: CommandLineRunner is an interface used to execute code after the Spring Boot application starts successfully. It is often used for initialization tasks, data seeding, startup validation, or background setup operations. Unlike ApplicationRunner, it receives command-line arguments as a simple String array. Multiple CommandLineRunner implementations can exist in the same application and their execution order can be controlled using the @Order annotation. It is commonly used when startup logic needs to run automatically during application initialization.

Que.q: Q15 : What is Spring Boot CLI and the most used CLI commands?
Que.a: Spring Boot CLI is a command-line tool that allows developers to create, run, and test Spring Boot applications quickly without setting up a complete project structure manually. It uses Groovy scripts and automatically resolves dependencies. The CLI is useful for rapid prototyping, learning Spring Boot, and creating simple applications. It reduces configuration effort and provides commands for running applications, checking versions, and managing projects. Although less common in production environments, it is valuable for development and experimentation.

Que.q: Q16 : What is Spring Boot dependency management?
Que.a: Spring Boot dependency management is a mechanism that automatically manages compatible versions of libraries and frameworks used in a project. Through the Spring Boot parent POM and starter dependencies, developers do not need to specify versions for most commonly used libraries. Spring Boot ensures that all dependencies work together correctly, reducing version conflicts and simplifying project maintenance. This approach saves development time, improves stability, and allows developers to focus on application development instead of dependency compatibility issues.

Que.note: Spring Boot manages dependency versions through spring-boot-dependencies BOM (Bill of Materials).

Que.q: Q17 : Is it possible to change the port of the embedded Tomcat server in Spring Boot?
Que.a: Yes, Spring Boot allows developers to change the default embedded Tomcat server port easily. The server port can be configured through application.properties, application.yml, environment variables, or command-line arguments. This flexibility helps when multiple applications need to run on the same machine or when deployment environments require custom ports. Spring Boot automatically starts the embedded server using the configured port during application startup. Changing the port requires no additional server configuration, making deployment and development more convenient.

Que.q: Q18 : What happens if a starter dependency includes conflicting versions of libraries with other dependencies in the project?
Que.a: When conflicting library versions exist, Spring Boot's dependency management mechanism attempts to resolve the conflict by selecting the version defined in its managed dependency set. This ensures compatibility across commonly used libraries. However, if developers explicitly specify another version, Maven or Gradle dependency resolution rules may override Spring Boot's choice. Dependency conflicts can lead to runtime errors, class loading issues, or unexpected behavior. Tools such as Maven Dependency Tree and Gradle Dependency Insight help identify and resolve version conflicts effectively.

Que.note: Use Maven dependency:tree or Gradle dependencies command to identify version conflicts.

Que.q: Q19 : What is the default port of Tomcat in Spring Boot?
Que.a: The default port used by the embedded Apache Tomcat server in Spring Boot is 8080. When a Spring Boot web application starts, it automatically launches Tomcat and listens for incoming HTTP requests on port 8080 unless another port is configured. This default setting allows developers to run applications immediately without additional server setup. If port 8080 is already occupied, the application will fail to start unless a different port is specified through configuration properties or environment settings.

Que.q: Q20 : Can we disable the default web server in a Spring Boot application?
Que.a: Yes, Spring Boot allows developers to disable the embedded web server when building non-web applications such as batch jobs, command-line tools, or background processing services. This can be achieved by setting the application type to NONE or excluding web-related auto-configurations. Disabling the server reduces resource usage and startup overhead because no servlet container is initialized. It is useful when an application does not expose HTTP endpoints and only performs internal processing tasks.

Que.q: Q21 : How to disable a specific auto-configuration class?
Que.a: Spring Boot allows developers to disable specific auto-configuration classes when the default configuration is not required. This can be useful when an application needs custom configurations or when certain auto-configured components cause conflicts. Auto-configuration can be disabled using the exclude attribute of @SpringBootApplication or @EnableAutoConfiguration. By excluding unnecessary configurations, developers gain greater control over application behavior and startup configuration while still benefiting from Spring Boot's automatic setup capabilities.

Que.q: Q22 : Can we create a non-web application in Spring Boot?
Que.a: Yes, Spring Boot can be used to create non-web applications such as batch processing systems, command-line tools, scheduled jobs, and background services. In such applications, there is no need to start an embedded web server like Tomcat. Spring Boot provides support through CommandLineRunner and ApplicationRunner interfaces for executing startup logic. By configuring the application as a non-web application, resource consumption is reduced while still taking advantage of Spring Boot features such as dependency injection, configuration management, and auto-configuration.

Que.q: Q23 : Describe the flow of HTTPS requests through a Spring Boot application.
Que.a: When an HTTPS request reaches a Spring Boot application, the SSL/TLS handshake is performed first to establish a secure connection between the client and server. After encryption is established, the request is received by the embedded server such as Tomcat. Spring Security filters process authentication and authorization checks before the request reaches the controller. The controller handles the business logic and generates a response. Finally, the response is encrypted and sent back to the client through the secure HTTPS connection.

Que.q: Q24 : Explain @RestController annotation in Spring Boot.
Que.a: @RestController is a specialized Spring annotation used for building RESTful web services. It combines the functionality of @Controller and @ResponseBody into a single annotation. Methods inside a @RestController automatically return data such as JSON or XML directly in the HTTP response body instead of rendering a view. This makes it ideal for REST APIs where data exchange is required between clients and servers. It simplifies API development and reduces the need for additional response handling configurations.

Que.q: Q25 : Difference between @Controller and @RestController
Que.a: @Controller is primarily used for traditional Spring MVC applications where views such as JSP, Thymeleaf, or HTML pages are returned. @RestController is used for REST APIs and automatically returns response data in formats like JSON or XML. While @Controller often requires @ResponseBody to return data directly, @RestController includes this functionality by default. As a result, @RestController is preferred for API development, whereas @Controller is commonly used for server-side rendered web applications.

Que.q: Q26 : What is the difference between RequestMapping and GetMapping?
Que.a: @RequestMapping is a generic annotation that can map requests for any HTTP method such as GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE. Developers must explicitly specify the request method when needed. @GetMapping is a specialized shortcut annotation introduced for handling only HTTP GET requests. It improves readability and reduces boilerplate code. While both annotations can be used for GET operations, @GetMapping is generally preferred because it clearly communicates the intent of the endpoint and makes controller code easier to understand.

Que.q: Q27 : What are the differences between @SpringBootApplication and @EnableAutoConfiguration annotation?
Que.a: @EnableAutoConfiguration enables Spring Boot's automatic configuration mechanism, allowing Spring to configure beans based on project dependencies and classpath settings. @SpringBootApplication is a convenience annotation that combines @EnableAutoConfiguration, @Configuration, and @ComponentScan into a single annotation. It serves as the primary annotation for Spring Boot applications. While @EnableAutoConfiguration focuses only on automatic configuration, @SpringBootApplication provides a complete application setup including configuration definition and component scanning along with auto-configuration support.

Que.q: Q28 : How can you programmatically determine which profiles are currently active in a Spring Boot application?
Que.a: Spring Boot provides the Environment interface to access application properties and active profiles programmatically. Developers can inject the Environment bean and call getActiveProfiles() to retrieve the currently active profiles. This is useful when application behavior needs to change dynamically based on the environment, such as development, testing, or production. Active profiles help manage environment-specific configurations while keeping a single codebase. Programmatic access allows custom logic and diagnostics based on profile information during runtime.

Que.q: Q29 : Mention the differences between WAR and embedded containers.
Que.a: A WAR file is deployed to an external application server such as Tomcat, JBoss, or WebLogic, where the server is managed separately from the application. Embedded containers, on the other hand, package the server directly inside the Spring Boot application. This allows the application to run independently using a simple JAR file. Embedded containers simplify deployment, reduce configuration complexity, and support microservices architectures. WAR deployments are more common in traditional enterprise environments where centralized application servers are already available.

Que.q: Q30 : What is Spring Boot Actuator?
Que.a: Spring Boot Actuator is a production-ready feature that provides monitoring, management, and health-check capabilities for Spring Boot applications. It exposes various endpoints that allow developers and administrators to inspect application health, metrics, beans, environment properties, thread information, and configuration details. Actuator is widely used for application monitoring, troubleshooting, and integration with monitoring tools such as Prometheus and Grafana. It helps improve application observability and enables proactive management of applications running in production environments.

Que.q: Q31 : How to enable Actuator in Spring Boot?
Que.a: Spring Boot Actuator can be enabled by adding the spring-boot-starter-actuator dependency to the project. Once added, Spring Boot automatically configures management endpoints that provide information about application health, metrics, beans, environment properties, and more. Developers can further customize which endpoints are exposed using configuration properties. Actuator is widely used in production environments for monitoring, troubleshooting, and integrating applications with observability tools. It helps administrators understand application behavior and detect issues before they impact users.

Que.q: Q32 : How to get the list of all the beans in our Spring Boot application?
Que.a: Spring Boot provides multiple ways to view all beans registered in the application context. Developers can use the ApplicationContext object and retrieve bean names programmatically. Another common approach is enabling the Actuator beans endpoint, which exposes all configured beans through a REST endpoint. Viewing beans is useful for debugging dependency injection issues, understanding application configuration, and verifying that required components have been loaded successfully. This information can be especially valuable when working with large enterprise applications.

Que.q: Q33 : Can we check the environment properties in our Spring Boot application? Explain how.
Que.a: Yes, Spring Boot allows developers to access environment properties through the Environment interface or the Actuator environment endpoint. Environment properties include application settings, system properties, environment variables, and profile-specific configurations. These properties can be read programmatically for dynamic application behavior. Additionally, the Actuator /env endpoint can expose configuration details for monitoring and troubleshooting purposes. Accessing environment properties helps developers verify configuration values and diagnose deployment issues across different environments.

Que.q: Q34 : How to enable debugging log in the Spring Boot application?
Que.a: Spring Boot provides built-in support for debug logging, which helps developers analyze application startup behavior and troubleshoot configuration issues. When debug mode is enabled, Spring Boot displays detailed information about auto-configuration decisions, bean creation, and application initialization. This feature is particularly useful for diagnosing dependency injection problems and understanding why certain configurations are applied or skipped. Debug logs can be enabled through configuration files, command-line arguments, or application startup parameters without changing application code.

Que.q: Q35 : Explain the need of dev-tools dependency.
Que.a: Spring Boot DevTools is a development-time dependency designed to improve developer productivity. It provides features such as automatic application restart, live reload support, improved development caching, and faster feedback during coding. Whenever source code changes are detected, DevTools automatically restarts the application, eliminating the need for manual restarts. This significantly reduces development time and improves the overall development experience. DevTools is intended only for development environments and should not be included in production deployments.

Que.q: Q36 : How do you test a Spring Boot application?
Que.a: Testing a Spring Boot application typically involves unit testing, integration testing, and end-to-end testing. Unit tests verify individual classes and methods in isolation, while integration tests validate interactions between components such as controllers, services, and databases. Spring Boot provides testing support through Spring Boot Test, JUnit, Mockito, MockMvc, and Testcontainers. Automated testing ensures application reliability, detects regressions early, and improves code quality. A well-tested application is easier to maintain and more resilient to future changes.

Que.q: Q37 : What is the purpose of unit testing in software development?
Que.a: Unit testing focuses on verifying the correctness of individual units of code, such as methods or classes, in isolation from the rest of the application. The primary purpose is to ensure that each component behaves as expected under different conditions. Unit tests help identify defects early, improve code quality, simplify refactoring, and provide confidence when making changes. Because they execute quickly and automatically, unit tests are an essential part of modern software development and continuous integration practices.

Que.note: Good unit tests should be fast, independent, repeatable, and easy to maintain.

Que.q: Q38 : How do JUnit and Mockito facilitate unit testing in Java projects?
Que.a: JUnit and Mockito are widely used testing frameworks in Java projects. JUnit provides annotations, assertions, and test execution capabilities that help developers write and organize test cases efficiently. Mockito complements JUnit by creating mock objects that simulate dependencies, allowing classes to be tested in isolation. Together, they enable developers to verify business logic without relying on databases, external APIs, or complex infrastructure. This combination leads to faster tests, improved maintainability, and more reliable software development practices.

Que.q: Q39 : Explain the difference between @Mock and @InjectMocks in Mockito.
Que.a: @Mock is used to create mock objects for dependencies, allowing developers to simulate their behavior during testing. @InjectMocks is used to create the class under test and automatically inject the mocked dependencies into it. Together, these annotations simplify test setup and reduce boilerplate code. While @Mock defines the fake collaborators, @InjectMocks prepares the actual object being tested. This combination is commonly used in service layer testing where dependencies such as repositories or external clients need to be mocked.

Que.q: Q40 : What is the role of @SpringBootTest annotation?
Que.a: @SpringBootTest is a testing annotation that loads the complete Spring application context during test execution. It is commonly used for integration testing because it allows developers to verify how different components work together within the application. Unlike simple unit tests, @SpringBootTest initializes beans, configurations, and auto-configurations exactly as they would run in production. This helps validate application behavior in a realistic environment and ensures that controllers, services, repositories, and other components integrate correctly.

Que.q: Q41 : How do you handle exceptions in Spring Boot applications?
Que.a: Exception handling in Spring Boot is used to manage application errors gracefully and provide meaningful responses to users. Spring Boot allows handling exceptions using try-catch blocks, @ExceptionHandler methods, @ControllerAdvice, and custom exception classes. Global exception handling ensures consistent error responses across the application. Proper exception handling improves debugging, maintainability, and user experience by preventing stack traces from being exposed to clients and returning appropriate HTTP status codes.

Que.q: Q42 : Explain the purpose of the pom.xml file in a Maven project.
Que.a: The pom.xml file is the core configuration file of a Maven project. It contains project metadata, dependencies, plugins, build configurations, repositories, and project version information. Maven reads this file to download required libraries, compile code, run tests, and package the application. In Spring Boot projects, pom.xml also manages starter dependencies and build plugins. Proper configuration of pom.xml helps maintain consistency, simplifies dependency management, and automates the project build lifecycle.

Que.q: Q43 : How auto configuration play an important role in Spring Boot application?
Que.a: Auto-configuration is one of the most important features of Spring Boot. It automatically configures beans and application settings based on the dependencies available on the classpath. Developers do not need to write large amounts of XML or Java configuration manually. For example, adding spring-boot-starter-web automatically configures Tomcat, DispatcherServlet, and related components. Auto-configuration reduces development time, minimizes boilerplate code, and allows developers to focus on business logic rather than infrastructure setup.

Que.note: Auto-configuration works using @EnableAutoConfiguration and conditional annotations such as @ConditionalOnClass and @ConditionalOnMissingBean.

Que.q: Q44 : Can we customize a specific auto-configuration in Spring Boot?
Que.a: Yes, Spring Boot allows customization of auto-configuration. Developers can override default bean definitions by creating their own beans, changing application properties, or excluding specific auto-configuration classes. Spring Boot gives priority to user-defined configurations over automatically configured beans. This flexibility allows developers to use the convenience of auto-configuration while still customizing application behavior according to business requirements. It helps balance rapid development with complete control over the application's configuration.

Que.q: Q45 : How can you disable specific auto-configuration classes in Spring Boot?
Que.a: Specific auto-configuration classes can be disabled when they are not required by the application. Spring Boot provides the exclude attribute of @SpringBootApplication or @EnableAutoConfiguration to prevent certain configurations from loading. This is useful when developers want full control over component configuration or when default behavior conflicts with custom requirements. Disabling unnecessary auto-configurations can also reduce startup time and avoid creating unwanted beans in the application context.

Que.q: Q46 : What is the purpose of having a spring-boot-starter-parent?
Que.a: spring-boot-starter-parent is a special parent POM provided by Spring Boot that simplifies Maven project configuration. It manages compatible versions of common dependencies, plugins, and build settings. Developers do not need to specify versions for most Spring Boot dependencies because they are automatically managed. This reduces dependency conflicts and ensures stability. It also provides sensible defaults for compiler settings, testing frameworks, and packaging options, making project setup faster and more reliable.

Que.q: Q47 : How do starters simplify the Maven or Gradle configuration?
Que.a: Spring Boot starters are preconfigured dependency bundles that simplify project setup. Instead of manually adding multiple related libraries, developers can add a single starter dependency that includes all required components. For example, spring-boot-starter-web includes Spring MVC, embedded Tomcat, validation libraries, and JSON support. Starters reduce dependency management complexity, prevent version conflicts, and provide a faster way to start application development while following Spring Boot best practices.

Que.q: Q48 : How do you create REST APIs?
Que.a: REST APIs in Spring Boot are created using @RestController, request mapping annotations, service classes, and data repositories. The controller receives HTTP requests and returns responses in JSON or XML format. Common annotations such as @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, and @DeleteMapping are used to implement CRUD operations. Spring Boot automatically handles request processing, serialization, and dependency injection. This makes API development simple, scalable, and suitable for web, mobile, and microservice applications.

Que.q: Q49 : What is versioning in REST? What are the ways that we can use to implement versioning?
Que.a: REST API versioning is the practice of maintaining multiple API versions while ensuring backward compatibility. It allows applications to evolve without breaking existing clients. Versioning becomes important when API contracts change over time. Spring Boot supports different versioning approaches such as URI versioning, request parameter versioning, custom header versioning, and content negotiation. Choosing a suitable versioning strategy helps manage API evolution, maintain compatibility, and provide a smooth migration path for consumers.

Que.q: Q50 : What are the REST API Best Practices?
Que.a: REST API best practices help create scalable, secure, and maintainable services. APIs should use meaningful resource names, proper HTTP methods, standard status codes, and consistent response formats. Security should be implemented using HTTPS, authentication, and authorization mechanisms. Proper validation, pagination, filtering, documentation, and versioning should also be included. Error responses should be meaningful and consistent. Following these practices improves developer experience, application reliability, and long-term maintainability of RESTful services.

Que.q: Q58 : What are the different Spring Boot annotations?
Que.a: Spring Boot provides many important annotations that simplify application development, configuration, dependency injection, REST API creation, scheduling, and asynchronous processing. Some of the most commonly used Spring Boot annotations are listed below :

list.@SpringBootApplication: Combines @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration, and @ComponentScan. Used to bootstrap and start a Spring Boot application.
list.@EnableAutoConfiguration: Automatically configures Spring Boot based on dependencies available in the classpath.
list.@Configuration: Marks a class as a source of bean definitions for the Spring container.
list.@ComponentScan: Scans and registers Spring-managed components automatically.
list.@Bean: Explicitly creates and manages a bean inside the Spring container.
list.@Component: Marks a class as a generic Spring-managed component.
list.@Service: Marks a class as a service layer component containing business logic.
list.@Repository: Marks a class as a data access component and provides exception translation.
list.@Controller: Handles web requests and returns views.
list.@RestController: Combines @Controller and @ResponseBody to return JSON/XML responses directly.
list.@RequestMapping: Maps HTTP requests to controller methods.
list.@GetMapping: Maps HTTP GET requests to a specific method.
list.@PostMapping: Maps HTTP POST requests to a specific method.
list.@PutMapping: Maps HTTP PUT requests to a specific method.
list.@DeleteMapping: Maps HTTP DELETE requests to a specific method.
list.@RequestParam: Binds request parameters to method arguments.
list.@PathVariable: Extracts values from URI path variables.
list.@RequestBody: Converts request body data into a Java object.
list.@ResponseBody: Returns method output directly as the HTTP response body.
list.@Qualifier: Specifies which bean should be injected when multiple beans of the same type exist.
list.@Value: Injects values from properties files, environment variables, or expressions.
list.@Profile: Activates beans only for specific environments such as dev, test, or prod.
list.@ConfigurationProperties: Binds external configuration properties to Java objects.
list.@Scheduled: Runs methods automatically at fixed intervals or cron schedules.
list.@Async: Executes methods in a separate thread asynchronously.
list.@ExceptionHandler: Handles exceptions thrown by controller methods.
list.@ControllerAdvice: Provides global exception handling across multiple controllers.
list.@CrossOrigin: Enables Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) for APIs.
list.@EnableWebMvc: Enables and customizes Spring MVC configuration.
list.@SpringBootTest: Loads the complete Spring application context for integration testing.
list.@MockBean: Creates and injects mock beans for testing purposes.
